title: From Tokenmaxxing to Trusted Throughput — Mingsheng Hong, Ironclad

summary:
Mingsheng Hong, VP of Engineering for AI at Ironclad, opens with cautionary industry examples including an Amazon engineer-built token leaderboard and reports of a $500M monthly cloud spend, then argues any organization faces the same risks. The first operational lesson is to track per-team and per-individual token cost and usage while treating the dashboard as a smoke detector, not a leaderboard; suspiciously low usage is worth investigating and high usage should never be rewarded. He cautions that adoption must precede cost control. He then addresses craft loss, urging leaders to surface the high-judgment, high-impact work that lets engineers still grow.

Ironclad builds AI for legal contracting where trust is the dominant product constraint, and the same ladder motivates their engineering metric: trusted throughput, defined across three buckets of objective checks, subjective human review, and customer-visible outcomes. To measure cost they aggregate vendor analytics across multiple coding tools, but warn against jumping from measurement to cost reduction; ROI requires measuring value too. Their value metric evolved from lines of code to open pull requests, to merged PRs, and now to merged PRs weighted by an AI-assigned complexity t-shirt size, because a 10-line concurrency fix outweighs 1000 lines of boilerplate. He warns against optimizing either LOC or tokens.

Hong identifies the new bottlenecks in code review and CI: when regression tests take an hour, engineers stop splitting PRs and submit large ones, making human review harder. Ironclad's response is unglamorous: AI handles the first review pass, humans apply deep judgment on architecture and security, and the platform team invests in killing flaky tests, improving CI infrastructure, and measuring ready-to-merged wait time and retry counts. He closes with a pragmatic framework covering guardrails, anomaly alerts, prompt caching, context pruning, and a build-versus-buy principle that buys non-differentiating infrastructure and builds internal prompt playbooks for context-specific workflows, ending with a hiring note.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Token leaderboards and the smoke detector framing
sections.summary: Hong opens with sensational industry stories including an Amazon token leaderboard, a Meta analogue, and a reported $500M monthly cloud spend, then argues that any organization faces the same risks. He introduces the smoke-detector framing: track every team's and individual's cost, but treat suspiciously low usage as a signal to investigate and never reward high usage.

sections.title: Adoption before austerity
sections.summary: He cautions that this talk is for teams past the AI adoption hump; organizations still provisioning access and encouraging first use are not ready for cost control. He describes the craft-loss concern from engineers who used to take pride in handcrafted code and now review AI slop, urging leaders to surface the high-judgment work that still lets engineers grow.

sections.title: Trust as Ironclad's product constraint
sections.summary: Ironclad builds AI features for legal contracting where trust is the top priority; lawyers test outputs on familiar contracts before expanding use. Hong draws the parallel to engineering: gaining trust from internal engineers, leadership, and customers is the same ladder that motivates their internal productivity metric.

sections.title: Trusted throughput as ROI proxy
sections.summary: Hong reframes the goal away from austerity and toward improving ROI of token spend. Trusted throughput is defined as code that has been reviewed, validated internally, and validated in customer deployments. He describes measuring cost by aggregating vendor analytics across multiple coding tools using AI-built pipelines and dashboards.

sections.title: The premature cut: measuring value alongside cost
sections.summary: He warns against jumping from cost measurement directly to cost reduction. ROI requires measuring value too, after which teams can find and fix bottlenecks. He previews that the new bottlenecks sit downstream in code review and CI/CD because code generation is now abundant. He also flags that team context matters when comparing usage, and that dashboard review feeds a self-learning loop for institutional best practices.

sections.title: LOC analogy and metric evolution to weighted merges
sections.summary: Using lines of code as an analogy, he argues LOC is worth tracking but terrible to optimize because deleting code is often better. Similarly, token spend should be tracked, not directly optimized. He then walks through the metric evolution: LOC, then open PRs, then merged PRs, then merged PRs weighted by a complexity score produced by prompting one or two LLMs to assign t-shirt sizes, because a 10-line concurrency fix is not equivalent to 1000 lines of boilerplate.

sections.title: Three buckets of trusted throughput
sections.summary: He sketches the qualitative definition of trusted throughput across three buckets: objective metrics such as test coverage, security checks, and canarying; subjective human judgment via code and design review covering quality, clarity, and architecture fit; and customer-visible outcomes such as rollbacks, complaints, and friction tickets. The section ends mid-thought as the three buckets come together to form the definition.

sections.title: Bottleneck shift to review and CI after AI abundance
sections.summary: Hong applies the trusted throughput lens to the SDLC and observes that AI makes PR creation abundant, so bottlenecks move downstream to review and CI. He warns against an anti-pattern where slow CI leads engineers to stop splitting PRs and submit large ones, raising review overhead and degrading review quality. Ironclad's code review principle is to onboard AI as the first level of defense for style and missing test coverage so that human reviewers can focus their deep judgment on architecture, security, and overall code quality, with humans retaining final accountability.

sections.title: CI pressure, flaky tests, and developer-experience metrics
sections.summary: He turns to CI/CD and notes that smaller, more frequent PRs driven by AI put real pressure on CI infrastructure, forcing engineers to waste human time babysitting flaky tests via manual reruns or to recruit AI agents to loop and retry, which wastes tokens and lowers morale. Ironclad invests developer-experience platform engineering into removing flaky tests and improving CI, and defines metrics such as the work-clock time from when a PR is ready to submit until it is actually submitted, and the number of times a PR must be retried to pass tests, treating a multi-hour ready-to-submit gap as a red flag.

sections.title: Pragmatic framework: guardrails, prompts, and efficiency habits
sections.summary: Hong shares a pragmatic framework with three aspects: guardrails around budgets, quotas, anomaly alerts, and a learning loop in which leadership reviews metrics with individuals to refine practices; continued search for AI best practices such as capping agentic retry loops after the initial PR so runaway loops do not burn tokens, and using prompt caching by structuring prompts with a fixed system prefix on top and varying content below; and context pruning as muscle memory, summarized across long sessions and supported by tools like Claude Code that auto-compact context to improve both token efficiency and output quality.

sections.title: Build versus buy, lessons, and closing
sections.summary: He closes with a build-versus-buy principle: buy non-differentiating infrastructure like IDE and CI, but build internal prompt playbooks for context-specific work such as generating high-quality PRs for small bug fixes, refactors, and new UI features. He notes some cases, like a cloud-based builder agent wrapping Claude Code, remain ambiguous and invites community exchange. His three summarizing lessons are to learn from others' mistakes, plan ahead for the impact of AI code generation on review and CI, and instrument the system to measure CI health and overall developer experience. He ends by calling this the golden era of AI where maximizing token ROI is the key to team success and notes Ironclad is hiring.

demonstrations: Cross-vendor cost aggregation using AI-built pipelines and dashboards to correlate token usage across multiple coding tools
Using a well-crafted AI prompt on one or two LLMs to assign t-shirt-size complexity scores to merged pull requests
AI as the first-level code reviewer handling style and test-coverage checks before routing to human reviewers
Workaround loop where an agent retries failing tests and auto-fixes code, capped by a step limit
Prompt structure with fixed system prompt on top and varying user content below to exploit vendor prefix caching
limitations: Complexity score for PRs has no traditional definition; Ironclad took a pragmatic prompt-based approach and is still evolving the metric
Teams still in the AI adoption phase are explicitly noted as not ready to apply the cost-control framework
Build-versus-buy calls can be ambiguous case-by-case; Ironclad is still evaluating a cloud-based builder agent against external vendors

organization.name: Ironclad
organization.summary: Ironclad is an independent San Francisco company that builds AI contract lifecycle management software for legal, procurement, and business teams. First-party pages describe an AI CLM platform for creating, reviewing, signing, storing, analyzing, and fulfilling contracts, with native AI for drafting, redlining, clause detection, and insights, plus Jurist as an agentic contract assistant. The about page records founding in 2014 by attorney Jason Boehmig and engineer Cai GoGwilt, Y Combinator origins, and Dan Springer as CEO since 2025. Mingsheng Hong is VP of Engineering focused on AI there and presents Ironclad's internal trusted-throughput practices for coding-agent token spend. Amazon and Meta appear only as cautionary industry stories, not as implementation owners.
organization.status: Independent private company as of the research date. Homepage, about page, AI CLM product page, and developer.ironcladapp.com are live. About page states Dan Springer became CEO in 2025 and the platform has processed two billion contracts. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
